patient.chief_complaint: Progressive behavioral changes and judicial performance decline — 28 months; referred by occupational health after judicial performance review
patient.history_present_illness: The Honorable Judge W is a 63-year-old retired judge who presents with her husband of 36 years. The referral comes from the occupational health physician of the judicial system, who describes a 28-month history of progressive behavioral and professional decline that led to a confidential judicial performance review and ultimately to her retirement 18 months ago. Her husband is the primary historian as she dismisses all concerns with judicial formality, stating she 'retired on her own terms' and 'has no medical problems worth discussing.' Her husband reports that the behavioral changes began approximately 28 months ago, initially attributed to the stress of a high-profile murder case. She began making errors in legal proceedings that were out of character — contradicting written rulings made minutes earlier, making statements to litigants that her colleagues found highly inappropriate, and once dismissing a case for a reason that had no legal basis. Outside the courtroom, she began purchasing identical items online without recollection — 14 dresses, 22 identical coffee mugs, and several expensive collectibles she had no prior interest in. She made sexually suggestive comments to a church elder in front of congregation members, causing a significant incident. She has developed a fixed daily routine and becomes highly distressed when any element is altered. She repeats the same three stories at dinner parties, word for word, without awareness of repetition. She has lost interest in her family's activities and shows no emotional engagement with her grandchildren whom she previously adored. Her mother has Alzheimer's disease (diagnosed at age 72 — currently in memory care). Her brother has uncharacterized memory complaints. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c on recent check) and hypertension — both vascular risk factors that could contribute to white matter disease. She has well-controlled hypothyroidism. The DIAGNOSTIC TRAP in this case: (1) family history of maternal AD raises familial Alzheimer's concern; (2) vascular risk factors raise vascular dementia; (3) the behavioral syndrome (disinhibition, perseveration, loss of empathy) is FTD pattern, not AD pattern. The key investigation that resolves the case: negative amyloid PET excludes maternal AD inheritance; FDG-PET frontal pattern excludes vascular dementia.

output.query: bvFTD vascular dementia FDG-PET differentiation frontal white matter Fazekas

results.title: FDG-PET distinguishes bvFTD from vascular dementia: frontal vs subcortical-frontal metabolic patterns

output.summary: Vascular dementia (subcortical small vessel type) produces a characteristic FDG-PET pattern of subcortical and periventricular hypometabolism corresponding to white matter hyperintensities, with relative preservation of cortical metabolism. The degree of metabolic change is generally proportional to the volume of white matter lesions. Fazekas grade 2 changes alone are associated with modest subcortical hypometabolism rather than severe cortical frontal hypometabolism. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Frontotemporal dementia in professional occupations: occupational performance and ethical implications

output.summary: Frontotemporal dementia in professionals with decision-making authority (judges, physicians, attorneys, executives) creates unique ethical and legal issues. Key considerations include formal capacity assessment, establishment of durable power of attorney (financial and healthcare), driving safety assessment, and confidential disclosure to oversight bodies depending on jurisdiction. Clinical correlation and legal consultation recommended.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Definitively exclude AD with amyloid PET given strong maternal AD history and APOE e4 concern.
Optimise vascular risk factors regardless of primary diagnosis.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
key_reasoning_points: Negative amyloid PET securely excludes AD as the primary aetiology despite strong family history and APOE e4.
Small-vessel changes contribute but do not explain the lobar frontotemporal pattern.
Address fiduciary capacity urgently for a sitting / recently retired judge.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors on familial AD as the explanation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of AD does not determine etiology; biomarkers (amyloid PET) are the discriminator.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle bvFTD — APOE e4 + maternal AD creates AD diagnostic trap; Fazekas 2 creates vascular dementia red herring. Key teaching: APOE e4 does NOT diagnose AD; negative amyloid PET definitively excludes AD regardless of family history; preserved posterior cingulate on FDG-PET is the single most discriminating AD-exclusion finding.
